title: From source file to running program
objective: By the end of this lesson you can name the four stages between your source file and an executable, inspect the output of each one, and tell from an error message which stage failed.

blocks.text: One command turns a text file into a program, which makes it easy to treat the whole thing as magic. It is four separate steps, each with its own input, output, and failure messages — and knowing which one failed is most of the work of fixing a build error.

blocks.caption: The pipeline
lines: hello.o        object file — machine code with unresolved names

blocks.caption: Stop after any step and look
lines: gcc -S hello.c -o hello.s    # stop after producing assembly
gcc -c hello.c -o hello.o    # compile and assemble, do not link
gcc hello.c -o hello         # all four stages
wc -l hello.c hello.i        # note how much #include pulled in

blocks.title: The preprocessor is only text
blocks.text: #include does not import a module — it pastes the entire contents of another file in place. #define does not create a constant — it replaces text before the compiler ever sees it. That is why a 5-line program can preprocess to tens of thousands of lines, and why a badly written macro produces errors that mention code you did not write.
Reading the error and knowing who produced it

rows: No such file or directory: stdio.h
Missing header or wrong include path
A syntax error in your C
You called something with no declaration in scope
It compiled, but nothing provides the actual function
The library is not installed or not on the search path

blocks.title: 'undefined reference' is a linker error, not a typo
blocks.text: It means the compiler accepted the call because a declaration existed, but at link time no object file or library actually contained the function. The usual causes are a missing source file in the build, or a library you did not link with -l. Reading the stage from the message saves you from searching your syntax for a problem that is not there.

rows: Turn on the warnings that catch real defects
Treat warnings as errors — common in real projects
Include debug information, so a debugger can show your source
No optimisation while learning / optimised for release
Compile to an object file without linking
Link against a library (m is the maths library)
Add runtime memory checking — you will use this later

blocks.title: Learn with -O0 -g
blocks.text: Optimisation rearranges and removes code, so a debugger shows lines executing out of order or variables that no longer exist. While you are learning, turn it off. Turn it back on when you measure performance, and be aware that optimisation can change what undefined behaviour does — a subject of its own lesson.

blocks.title: Take the pipeline apart
steps: Create hello.c:  #include <stdio.h>  then  int main(void){ printf("hi\n"); return 0; }
Run: gcc -E hello.c -o hello.i && wc -l hello.c hello.i    (how much came in)
Run: gcc -S hello.c -o hello.s && head -20 hello.s          (the assembly)
Run: gcc -c hello.c -o hello.o && file hello.o              (an object file)
Run: nm hello.o                                             (symbols: printf is undefined here)
Now break it on purpose: delete the #include and rebuild — read which stage complains
blocks.expected: A tiny source file expanding to a very large preprocessed file, then assembly, then an object file whose symbol table shows printf as unresolved until the linker supplies it. The deliberate break shows you the error message that belongs to a specific stage.

cheatsheet: Four stages: preprocess → compile → assemble → link
-E stops after preprocessing · -S after assembly · -c after the object file
#include pastes a whole file in; #define is text replacement before compiling
'expected ;' is the compiler · 'undefined reference' is the linker
undefined reference = declared but nothing provides it: missing file or missing -l
-g for debug info, -O0 while learning, -O2 for release
nm shows the symbols an object file defines and needs

checkpoint.prompt: What does the preprocessor actually do with #include <stdio.h> ?

choices.D: Pastes the entire contents of that header file into your source before compilation

checkpoint.explanation: It is text substitution. That is why a short program can preprocess into tens of thousands of lines.

checkpoint.prompt: You get 'undefined reference to sqrt'. Which stage failed and why?

choices.B: The linker — the declaration existed so it compiled, but no library or object file provided the function (here, missing -lm)

checkpoint.explanation: Declaration and definition are separate things in C. The header promised the function exists; the linker is the stage that has to find it.

choices.D: An object file: machine code with names that are not yet resolved

checkpoint.explanation: -c compiles and assembles but does not link, which is how multi-file projects are built before being joined together.

choices.A: It is required for -Wall to work
choices.B: Optimisation rearranges and removes code, so a debugger shows lines out of order and variables that no longer exist
choices.C: It makes the program run faster

checkpoint.explanation: You want the running program to match the source you are reading. Turn optimisation on when you are measuring performance, not while you are learning what the code does.
